kinds.d: Mined diamond, loose and cut, graded D to Z for colourless to light colour or as a natural fancy colour.

x.d: Diamond graded on the D (colourless) to Z (pale yellow or brown) scale, usually sold with a lab report.
x.dt: D–Z colour · cut, clarity and carat on the lab report · round brilliant to fancy shapes

x.d: Brown natural diamond sold under trade names: champagne for light brown, cognac for orangish brown, coffee for deep brown.

v.d: Light brown, even though the colour looks light yellow
Usually orangish brown
Usually deep or vivid brown

x.dt: fancy brown grades · Argyle supply made them plentiful from the 1980s

x.d: Pink and red diamond from the Argyle mine, Western Australia, the only significant source until mining ceased in November 2020.

v.d: Annual invitation-only sale of the best pink stones

x.dt: small stones · fancy pink grades · Argyle origin documented by tender

x.d: Intensely yellow diamond, traded as canary; yellow is the second most common fancy colour.
x.dt: fancy yellow grades from Fancy Light to Fancy Vivid

x.d: Blue diamond coloured by boron (type IIb), among the most valuable fancy colours.

v.d: 45.52-carat blue diamond from the Kollur mine, India
14.62-carat Fancy Vivid Blue sold for US$50.6 million

x.dt: type IIb · fancy blue grades · usually under 5 ct apart from famous stones

x.n: Fancy red, green, black and grey diamond
x.d: Rarer fancy-colour natural diamonds: red is the rarest, green is usually light, black is opaque, grey and milky white also graded.
x.dt: hue and saturation grading rather than D–Z

kinds.d: Diamond grown in a factory, chemically and physically the same as mined diamond, from near-colourless to fancy colours.

x.d: Grown from a carbon source dissolved in molten metal flux under high pressure and temperature on a diamond seed.

v.d: Tracy Hall achieved the first commercially successful synthesis on 16 December 1954
General Electric first grew gem-quality crystals, reported in 1971
The three press designs used for HPHT growth

x.dt: yellow (nitrogen) and blue (boron) as grown · metallic flux inclusions · cuboctahedral growth

x.d: Grown layer by layer from methane and hydrogen plasma in a vacuum chamber onto a seed plate.
x.dt: often brown as grown, then HPHT-annealed to colourless · tabular crystals · even colour and strain banding

x.n: Treated pink and green lab-grown diamond
x.d: Fancy pink and green lab-grown stones made by irradiation (and heating) after growth.
x.dt: post-growth treatment · laser inscription of the girdle on major labs' reports

kinds.d: Synthetic ruby, sapphire, emerald, spinel and similar gems grown by flame fusion, flux or hydrothermal methods; the same material as the natural gem.

x.d: Synthetic ruby, sapphire and padparadscha made by melting powder in an oxyhydrogen flame and crystallising a boule.

v.d: Possibly the first flame-fusion rubies
Synthetic star sapphires made by Linde Air Products
Details of the process published

x.dt: curved growth lines and gas bubbles · cheapest method · boules cut into stones

x.d: Flux-grown synthetic emerald, ruby and sapphire from Carroll Chatham's San Francisco laboratory, the first marketable synthetic emerald.

v.d: Produced by Carroll Chatham
Credited to Carroll Chatham for flux growth of corundum

x.dt: slow growth from molten flux · lithium vanadate flux likely for emerald · no water in the stone

x.d: Flux-grown emerald from Pierre Gilson Sr., on the market since 1964, grown on coated natural colourless beryl seeds.
x.dt: seed crystals grown at about 1 mm a month · flux method

x.d: Emerald grown from hot aqueous solution under pressure, from thin layers on beryl seeds to fully synthetic crystals.

v.d: Thin emerald layers on natural colourless beryl, from Innsbruck
Fully synthetic hydrothermal emerald by Linde Division of Union Carbide
Sold as Colombian created emeralds

x.dt: hydrothermal · the method closest to natural formation

kinds.d: Stones that look like diamond but are not diamond: moissanite, cubic zirconia, white sapphire, historic YAG and GGG, glass and white zircon.

x.d: Lab-grown silicon carbide gem, harder than most simulants, doubly refractive and with more fire than diamond.

v.d: Charles & Colvard trademark, colour range D to K
Charles & Colvard trademark
Charles & Colvard trademark
Silicon carbide gems sold by other makers after patents expired by 2018

x.dt: Mohs 9.25 · birefringent · usually sold D–K colour

x.d: Cubic zirconium dioxide, the most important and cheapest diamond simulant since commercial production began in 1976.

v.d: Soviet name from the Lebedev institute (FIAN), skull-crucible technique
Ceres Corporation began mass production for jewellery
Swarovski is listed among major CZ producers as of 1993

x.dt: Mohs 8–8.5 · denser than diamond · more fire, duller facet edges · coloured and mystic-coated variants

x.d: Colourless synthetic corundum, made by the Verneuil process, used as a diamond simulant from 1900 to 1947.
x.dt: hardness 9 · looks lifeless next to diamond · flame-fusion boules

x.a: yttrium aluminium garnet · gadolinium gallium garnet
x.d: Yttrium aluminium garnet and gadolinium gallium garnet, colourless synthetic garnets used as diamond simulants in the 1970s.

v.d: Hardness 8.25, grown by the Czochralski process
Dispersion close to diamond, very dense, turns brown in UV

x.d: Mid-twentieth-century synthetic simulants with fire far above diamond but soft and tinted.

v.d: Slight yellow tint, doubly refractive, soft
Optics close to diamond but soft and brittle

x.d: Older imitations: lead glass paste (rhinestone, strass) from 1700 and natural colourless zircon.
x.dt: glass is very soft · white zircon is brittle and strongly birefringent

brands.d: Non-profit gemological institute and grading laboratory; set the D–Z colour scale used worldwide.
American Gem Society trade body with its own grading laboratory, AGS Laboratories, founded 1996.
International Gemological Institute; certifies diamonds, coloured stones and jewellery, widely used for lab-grown diamonds.
Swiss Gemmological Institute in Basel, part of the Swiss Foundation for Gemstone Research; origin reports for coloured stones and pearls.
Diamond laboratory in Antwerp, certifying diamonds.
Swiss laboratory known for coloured-stone origin reports.
Gemresearch Swisslab; coloured-stone and origin reports.
American Gemological Laboratories, New York; coloured-stone reports.
Company that produced and sold the first synthetic moissanite gems, introduced to jewellery in 1998.
Company founded by Carroll Chatham; first marketable synthetic emerald, also synthetic ruby and sapphire.
Crystal maker also listed among major cubic zirconia producers.
